# Āṭānāṭiya Sutta (DN 32 (PTS DN iii 194))

**ID:** DN 32 (PTS DN iii 194)
**Section:** Dīghanikāya (dn)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Āṭānāṭiya Sutta
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** The Āṭānāṭiya Protection
**PTS:** DN iii 194
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/dn32
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0103m.mul8.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Āṭānāṭiya Sutta* is the thirty-second discourse of the *Dīghanikāya* [Saha 1966; Goble 2012]. Set on Vulture's Peak near Rājagaha, the discourse opens as the Four Great Kings (*cātummahārājā* / *lokapāla*) arrive with their vast retinues of *yakkhas*, *gandhabbas*, *kumbhaṇḍas*, and *nāgas* [Goble 2012; Walker 2022]. Because not all non-human spirits are friendly to the Buddha's disciples, King Vessavaṇa (Vaiśravaṇa / Kuvera) recites the Āṭānāṭiya protective chant (*rakkhā*) for the monks' safeguarding, preceded by descriptions of the four directional realms—including the abundant northern continent of Uttarakuru—and invocations of past Buddhas [SuttaCentral; Goble 2012; Collins 1998; Walker 2022]. The commentary explains that the sutta takes its title from the celestial city of Āṭānāṭā mentioned within the text [Skilling 1993b]. Beyond its canonical status, the sutta developed an extensive liturgical afterlife: it forms the foundation of the popular *paritta* chant of the same name, appears in Southeast Asian ritual manuscripts such as Cambodian accordion leporellos, and served as an important precursor to later Buddhist apotropaic literature, including the *Mahāmāyūrī-sūtra* [Nakamura 1980; Walker 2022].

Parallels and related versions are attested across northern Buddhist traditions. Sanskrit manuscript fragments discovered in Central Asia, where the text is generally entitled *Ātānāṭika-sūtra*, were edited by Helmuth Hoffmann and studied by A. F. R. Hoernle, although they diverge substantially from the Pali text [Saha 1966; Nakamura 1980; Skilling 1992; Elverskog 1997]. Central Asian fragments are also preserved in Old Uygur [Elverskog 1997]. In Tibetan translation, the text is preserved in both a Mūlasarvāstivādin version (*D* 656) and a 14th-century Theravādin translation (*lCaṅ lo can gyi pho braṅ gi mdo*, *D* 33), both of which DharmaNexus aligns closely with the Pali sutta [Skilling 1992; Skilling 1993a; Skilling 1993b; DharmaNexus]. While absent from the Chinese *Dīrghāgama*, a separate Chinese translation is preserved as Taishō 1245 [Saha 1966; SuttaCentral]. Within Pali literature, DharmaNexus records widespread textual sharing with collections such as the *Aṅguttaranikāya* (AN 3, AN 4, AN 7, AN 10), the Vinaya *Mahākhandhaka*, and the *Pāthikavagga-aṭṭhakathā* [DharmaNexus].
